maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, November 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. 8, respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom-Mr. Bennett.-Mr. MacDonald (South Cape Breton) in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
We were considering
item 409.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
A few days ago I made
some remarks with regard to cream separators, and on that occasion the Prime Minister said that when the explanation was given I would probably be satisfied. I presume that the explanation that was then said to be forthcoming was that given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday. I can quite understand that the reasons advanced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce were satisfactory to the Prime Minister and perhaps quite satisfactory to both the British and Canadian manufacturers, but surely, Mr. Chairman, we must have failed completely to impress upon the government our point of view if the Prime Minister thinks that the reasons that have been advanced can be satisfactory to us.
The Prime Minister has said that this agreement was based upon and consistent with Conservative policy during the past two years; that is, the policy of protection. We are quite willing to admit that is true, and it is just because it is true that we object to this agreement in general and to this item in particular.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has told us that there would be no increase in price. His whole argument was based on the assumption that there would be no increase in price, but our objection to this item is that it will inevitably be followed by an increase in price. Just at that point we find the great difference between the position taken by the government and that taken by those on this side of the house. No increase in price? You will notice that the Minister of Trade and Commerce at page 1283 of Hansard said:
First, may I say that Canada will have access to other markets for cream separators. That should be borne in mind.

United Kingdom
How can we have access to other markets for cream separators when we are imposing a prohibitory tariff against separators coming in from other countries? I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this 25 per cent duty is a prohibitory tariff and will necessarily exclude the separators which are now coming to us from Sweden, Belgium and the United States. So how can it be said that we shall have access to other markets? The separators that are now coming to us from other countries cannot possibly climb over a 25 per cent tariff wall. If the foreigner should attempt to come in over that tariff wall by reducing his price, we know what the attitude of this government would be and has been to an attempt of that kind. It used to be contended that the foreigner would pay the duty.
So he does in many cases.

My hon. friend from Pictou says, "So he does," but the government take mighty good care that the foreigner does not pay the duty. If the foreigner tries to put an article into this country at a price lower than it is selling for in his own country and tries to absorb the tariff, this government takes care that that shall not be done. How can the Minister of Trade and Commerce say that we shall still have access to other markets? The contention of the government is that this 25 per cent tariff will not increase the price. Again let me point out as I did yesterday the inconsistency in the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite. They reduce the duties on cigarettes and liquor, and say that that will decrease the price. Possibly. Then they increase the duty on butter and say that that will increase the price. Then when it comes to barbed wire and cream separators, the imposition of a duty is to have no effect at all upon the price. That is the kind of argument we get from hon. gentlemen opposite. We maintain, Mr. Chairman, in spite of the assertions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that this 25 per cent duty will inevitably increase the price.
When some of these items have come before the committee and inquiries have been made as to the reason for the increased duty, the government has not been able to tell us from what quarter came the pressure for these new duties. In this instance we know from where the pressure came. According to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce it came from the Lister firm, which, according to the minister, were the first to introduce cream separators into Canada. Well, possibly that is true. I may be wrong in this point, but I remember a separator known as the Alexandra which, I think, the Lister company introduced. When that separator was first sold in our part of the country one could hear it running a mile away. There may be other separators from England with the details of which I am not familiar.

The statement by the
hon. member has been most unfair. Without accurate information under his hand he should not have made such a statement about a business concern.

I am simply stating the
fact.

No; the hon. member is
knocking a firm about which he knows nothing. He does not know whether or not his statements are accurate.
I am talking about separators introduced forty years ago.

I maintain that the hon.
member has made a most unfair statement.

Then, there is another
feature to this matter.
Oh, oh.
Order.

It is quite evident that one has no difficulty stirring up trouble in committee. I venture to say, however, that hon. members opposite who represent farming constituencies are just as much exercised over this matter as we are-and a good deal more.
Not one iota.

They are exercised not
only from the standpoint of the farmers' interests, but from that of the next election.
Not one iota.

I am old enough to remember when Sir John A. Macdonald introduced his national policy. The reason given at that time was that the policy was introduced to protect infant industries. So, down through the years we have listened to the contention that infant industries should be protected. Later we have heard the argument that we should continue protection of decrepit industries. The Prime Minister himself has indicated that possibly there may be certain industries to which, if we had to begin over again, we would not afford protective tariffs. Since those industries have been established however, and in view of the fact that they cannot be continued without protection, he
1288	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
proposes to support them. The position now is that while years ago we were asked to protect infant industries, we are now asked to protect inefficient industries.
But this agreement goes much farther than that. It asks us to protect not only infant industries in Canada but infant industries in Great Britain. It asks protection for industries which, perhaps for the reasons the minister lias mentioned, have been unable to supply the Canadian market. Mr. Chairman, I object strongly to that practice. So far as I know the demand has never come from this side of the house, and certainly never from the organized farmers of Manitoba whom I represent, that the British people should tax their food for our benefit. We have never made that demand. Indeed, hon. members on this side of the house have declared definitely that such a demand would not be for the welfare or unity of the empire. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think I can quite properly take the ground that we resent any demand from English manufacturers that we should impose an additional burden upon our farmers for the benefit of either a new industry or industries in Great Britain for which there is hope of revival. That is a strain to which we should not be subjected; it imposes on us too great a sacrifice for the promotion of empire unity.
Then there is a further matter that I should like to call to the attention of the minister. As a reason for its acceptance by the committee the minister urged that the changed tariff would help the export trade of manufacturers of cream separators. Ler us grant that that is true. That position however simply confirms us in the opinion we have expressed so frequently during this debate, namely, that this agreement was made not in the interests of consumers but in the interests of manufacturers and producers. Then, there is a further point to be taken into consideration in an agreement of this kind. We have heard a great deal about the demand for fair competition and fair opportunity to supply our own market. Let us see how this change intereferes with the right of farmers to have a fair opportunity in their own market. A few days ago I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question concerning the dumping duties which could be used by other dominions in the event of cream separators being sold there at a price lower than they were sold in Canada. He replied, of course, that nations would have dumping duties when their interests were adversely affected. Of course I expected that answer; perhaps he thought my question was

foolish. Nevertheless there is sometimes method in what appears to be madness.
Hear, hear.

The point I wish to bring out is that we are brought into competition with other producers of dairy products. We are told again and again that in the production of butter New Zealand has natural advantages over Canada. That is perfectly true. But that is no reason why, in addition to those natural advantages, New Zealand should have a further advantage over us brought about by an act, not of their own but of our government, and one which places us at an artificial disadvantage. I do not know what the duty on cream separators in New Zealand is, I have not had time to look up the information. But I venture to say that in a country Like New Zealand, whose products enter into competition with ours, their farmers, are not unduly handicapped by duties on cream separators. There may be small revenue duties, but I venture the assertion that farmers in that country are not handicapped by a heavy duty on cream separators; I venture the same assertion in regard to South Africa; I venture the same assertion in regard to Denmark. This last mentioned country is perhaps our chief competitor, at least one of our chief competitors, in dairy products in the British market. I venture to assert that the farmers of Denmark are not unduly handicapped in their business by duties placed upon cream separators.
This, Mr. Chairman, is an additional reason why we should oppose this item in the schedule, and why we lay so much emphasis upon it. Perhaps hon. members from other parts of the dominion, representing other industries, may not realize as much as we do the seriousness of this item. I do not think there is anything in the whole agreement which, from the standpoint of the great primary producer in Canada, is as objectionable as this most iniquitous tariff against cream separators.

Mr. Chairman, were I not to voice my protest against this item I should be neglecting my duty. Yesterday the minister stated that a man named Lister came into his office and intimated to him that Great Britain could supply cream separators to Canada. I have information before me from a firm doing a large business in cream separators in western Canada. Any information I have received previously from this firm has been authentic. In this instance their statement is that Great Britain does not make the cream separators, so-called, that farmers

United Kingdom
need for the separation of milk from cream. If the information this firm gives me is correct, and I feel certain it is, because the importations from Great Britain have been nil, we can arrive at no other conclusion than that the Canadian producer of dairy products will pay the extra duty of 25 per cent. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) mentioned that the reduction in excise on cigarettes and liquor had resulted in reduced prices. I can verify that, being quite a cigarette smoker myself; every time I buy a package of cigarettes I make a nickel.

You will make a lot
of money!

So if it works that way when the excise or duty is reduced it must work the other way when the duty is imposed or increased.
The information in this letter is, in part as follows:
About eight or ten months ago I saw a financial statement of an English company which manufactures and distributes butter and other dairy products and the statement also mentioned that they manufactured dairy and creamery equipment. I wrote for prices on cream separators and was told that they made only heavy power separators for creamery use and that the small separators for dairy farms were imported from Sweden.
I think it a great mistake to cut off the competition between domestic, American, Swedish and other countries in the matter of such a necessity of production as cream separators. We find that farmers are not able to buy separators now and complain that the cream cheques are so small that they cannot pay for the ones we have sold them.
I know of only two Canadian makes, the Renfrew, made in Renfrew, Ont., and the Massey-Harris, which, I suppose is made in Toronto.
What about De Laval?

He says he does not
know whether De Laval separators are made in Canada or not, but he knows that a few years ago De Laval imported separators into Canada and sold them to Canadian dairymen.

What is my hon. friend
quoting from?

I am quoting a letter
from a firm which does a large business selling separators to farmers in western Canada.
We would be better able to judge of the information if we had the name of the firm. I think we are entitled to the name. I gave my authority yesterday.

I expected that from the minister, and I am prepared for it. I am 53719-82
doing exactly what the minister and the right hon. Prime Minister have done; they read letter after letter without giving names. The Prime Minister even read a letter last year from a lady who commended him for reducing civil service salaries, and when he was asked to give the name he would not give it. I am just as much entitled to the privilege. The quotations I have given are from a letter from an authentic firm; any information they have given me has proved to be correct.
Do they manufacture- in Canada?

I am glad to see my hon. friend from Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), smile. If my hon. friend from Dufferin-Sim-coe and my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Senn), think they are going to play the same trick on the farmers in the next election, they are badly mistaken.
Order.

Well, I will withdraw the word trick," I will just say " playing the trick." I know my hon. friend from Dufferin Simcoe is too intelligent to broadcast to the farmers the imposition of this duty on cream separators. Now, Mr. Chairman, the purpose of these agreements is what? Nothing else than to benefit the manufacturing industries of this country. The producers and consumers of creamery or dairy products have never been consulted. The only people that have been consulted are English or Canadian manufacturers. That is what I say in western Canada and in all other parts of Canada. I ask of my friends from the eastern townships, where I spent my last week-end, those friends of mine from the eastern townships who slid into power on a pound of New Zealand butter: Are you going to tell your farmer friends who voted for you on that question that the government has done the very thing which is going to hamper the dairy industry to a greater degree than it is hampered today? In western Canada we are getting anywhere from 13 to 15 cents a pound for butter, and the minister and the government have to admit that the only reason for imposing this duty, if there is a reason, is either revenue or to protect the industry. When the duty becomes so high it ceases to bring revenue to the country, but it increases the price to the man who has to buy the commodity.

May I ask the hon. member, if the price of cream separators has increased? Is not the Massey-Harris separator as good as any in the country? I have had one for forty years.

1290	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
That is one of the old Listers you have got.
I am not concerned whether the price increased yesterday or today-
Oh, oh.

-but let me warn my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins) that he will never be able to go back to his county, with that cream can and the old cow, if he tells the people that the party that he supports, has increased the production costs of the dairyman. I know my hon. friend objects to this, but I can say, with all the respect I have for him, that if he goes back to the constituency of Marquette and repeats the argument he made in 1930 the old cow will not bawl, she will cry.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I plead with my farmer friends on the other side of the house, who in 1930 asked the farmers to support them; I plead with my personal friends from the eastern townships who I know contributed a great deal to the belief of the farmers that the Bennett government would give everything to the dairy industry and all would be well; I plead with these friends of mine now, and others, to stand up in this house and fight for the farmers' interests, knowing that if the farming industry does not become prosperous nothing will prosper in this country. As a final plea I ask my hon. friend from Dufferin-Simcoe, one of the best-looking men in this house, a man who is always smiling-I am only sorry he is not the Minister of Agriculture, because he is one of those back-benchers who would make a good Minister of Agriculture-to stand up in this house and tell this government that if they are going to impose these penalties on the farming industry, and especially the dairy industry, he is not going to support any such project.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Lisgar and the hon. member for Provencher each have made the bald statement that there will be an increase in cost, and they have based their whole complaint against these provisions upon that assumption.. If the cost is not increased then their argument is worthless.
Then why the duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The duty is for preference and for empire free trade in cream separators. Let me say this to my hon. friends: I take it that if they could get a separator at a given price they would prefer to buy it within the empire rather than without. They must assent to that position, otherwise they must take the ground that they prefer to buy from without rather than within the empire.

May I interrupt the
minister to tell him that if present conditions continue the farmers will not have money with which to buy separators from anyone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I only wish to say that I
do not assent for one moment to the proposition that these proposals will result in an increase in the cost of separators. We will find very fierce competition on the part of the British now that they have an opportunity in this market. But there is one point to which hon. gentlemen have not made reference; for many years past, with the exception of the bowl, every part imported for servicing cream separators had to pay a substantial duty, and under the provisions of this agreement these parts now come in free.
From where?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From within the empire.

But they do not come
in free from the United States or Sweden?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Just wait one second.
Under the tariff which was supported by my hon. friend from Provencher, when parts came in they were assessed at varying duties. For example, if made of iron or steel they would be dutiable under item 446, under which they paid 15 per cent under the British preference, 27| per cent under the intermediate and 35 per cent under the general tariff. If made of aluminum they paid 15 per cent under the British preference, 22! per cent under the intermediate and 25 per cent under the general tariff. If they were nickel plated they paid 30 per cent under the preferential tariff, 37! per cent under the intermediate tariff and 45 per cent under the general tariff. If made of copper or brass they paid a duty of 20 per cent under the preference, 27! per cent under the intermediate and 30 per cent under the general tariff. Now those preferential duties have been all swept away, and those parts can come in free.

I suppose the Minister of
Finance expects us to accept that argument as a valid reason for supporting this agreement. Probably the minister is stating the facts accurately with regard to the duty on imported parts, but supposing that tariff was in effect under the Liberal government, as he has suggested, and supported by members on this side of the house, is that any reason why the duty now should be imposed upon the complete article? Surely not. It does not make his case any better or our case any worse.

Certainly I am not going to let my genial friend the Minister of Finance get away with that. The minister is

United Kingdom
trying to impress upon the house the wonderful service being rendered the farmers of Canada by this government through the removal of the duty on cream separator parts. If his argument is sound; if it helps the farmers to take the duty off the parts, why put a duty on the finished article? Truly I cannot understand that reasoning. The government takes the duty off cream separator parts and gives that as an action that will benefit the consumer of cream separators. On the other hand it puts on a duty of 25 per cent on the finished article. I cannot understand that logic. Perhaps my brain is not working well this morning, though I went to bed fairly early last night.

I confess that it is very
difficult to follow the reasoning of some hon. gentlemen opposite. I suppose that one of the difficulties of our form of parliamentary procedure is-
The present government.

There we have another
illustration of it. It is simply impossible for us to reason out these things in a logical way and, shall I say, according to the facts, without interjecting partisan politics. I am not saying that my hon. friends opposite have a monopoly of this.
Oh, oh.

I quite agree with that.
So that my hon. friends will not accuse me for the next five minutes at least of being partisan, I grant that they have not a monopoly of that weakness or that fault, which is perhaps inherent to our system, but I should like to invite hon. gentlemen now to concentrate for a moment, in a logical way, upon this question.
You have not a monopoly of logic, either.
It is no use.

I grant you it is not. I
did not expect my hon. friend from Lisgar to interject a provocative statement at that moment. Can he not at least receive in the proper spirit the attempt I am making to approach the question from a business standpoint?
I do not think the minister will say that in my remarks I did anything but attempt to argue the question on valid, sound premises.

I did not name my hon. friend; I have been talking in generalities. I 53719-82*
am inviting the whole committee to consider this question from a logical standpoint rather than to allow our prejudices to interfere. I imagine it is hopeless, but I will go on. There are certain facts which I think the committee must bear in mind. The first is that as far as cream separators are concerned we now have free trade, if I might use that term, within the empire. That is, as far as Canada is concerned we have free access to the markets of the empire. That is of some value to Canada. I cannot agree with hon. gentlemen opposite when they suggest that we must look askance at some advantage to the industrialists of Canada. I think it is a desirable and commendable thing if that is secured. That is my position, and that is point numbei one.

Before the
minister leaves that point may I inquire if there ever has been any obstacle in the way of trade within the empire?

Yes; practically every
part of the empire had a duty on cream separators. Now we have free entry to those markets. Just on that point let us consider for a moment precisely what was the argument advanced by the Minister of Finance a moment ago. Let us look at this matter calmly and dispassionately. There have been duties. I am not blaming my hon. friends opposite at all, but as a matter of fact there have been duties on parts. The hon. member for Provencher asked a question which I think was very proper, but which I also think is very capable of being answered. He askf what that has to do with putting a duty or the finished article.
I did not say that.
I think I caught my hon friend correctly. He asked, if it was desirable to take the duty off parts, whether that was not a sound reason for taking the duty off the finished article.

No, that was not what I said. I took it that the Minister of Finance was arguing that the removal of the duty on parts was a benefit to the farmer. Then, if his argument was sound, I asked why the duty should be put on the finished article.

Quite so; that is what I had in mind, only I left out the word "farmer." That is quite right. There is an anwer and, I think, a valid answer to that. The manufacture of cream separators in Canada has been carried on by three firms for a very considerable number of years, but a substantial
1292	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
part of that manufacturing has been in the way of assembling. In nearly all industries there are some parts of machinery that can be made better elsewhere, because of the quantum factor, and such parts are brought in. Such items as bowls and some other things have been brought in as finished part3 and assembled with the other parts of Canada. Now, by the step we have taken in removing the duty from Great Britain at least on all these parts, we are contributing something towards lessening the assembling cost in Canada. That is axiomatic and I think it will be accepted in the discussion of industrial development.

If the taking off of the duty on parts that are made in foreign countries is an advantage to the cream separator producers in Canada, would it not work just as well if there were no duty on cream separators to the farmers?

If my hon. friend will follow me I will try to make that point clear. In the first place, the cream separator as such does come in free from Great Britain and remains free. But parts for repairs also come in free from Great Britain under the new arrangement we are making. If any large distributors wish to bring in repair parts- and I fancy that in all machinery there are certain parts that wear out before others do and consequently have to be brought in-* they will have those free from Great Britain; and they were not free before. Now, there is some compensation from that standpoint alone for the imposition of the duty on the finished article.
Was any substantial quantity of parts brought in from Great Britain before?
I gave the list last night.
In the list of imports which the minister gave last night are parts included?
I will have that in a moment. I am informed that the only parts that can be traced are bowls, of which some $24,000 worth were imported.
A list of imports was given last evening. Does that list include parts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Separators came in to the value of $455,000, and bowls, which have always been free, came in to the value of $24,000.
I would ask my hon. friend from Provencher, who I am glad to see has responded in a very nice spirit to my advances, to follow me.
My response is just until you finish your argument.

That is quite all right. At least I appreciate his temporary courtesy. There is this point which I would ask him and other hon. members to consider. In his remarks the hon. gentleman seemed to labour under the impression that there was in this nothing of any value for the farmer-that is, in the agreements or in our trade with Great Britain as represented in those agreements. Nothing at all. Well now, I invite him to consider this point. We are clear that under these agreements there are, for the producers of butter, cheese, powdered milk and so forth, all those things that are indigenous to the dairy industry, very definite and valuable preferences in the British market. The representatives of the British people say, "We are giving you these valuable concessions for your dairy industry in our market. Is it therefore not reasonable for you to give us a chance in your market with some of the machinery we produce and are able to supply you with?" That is not an illogical position to take; I submit that it is sound.
But I submit that you are putting under a handicap the producers of that very commodity on which you have a preference in Great Britain.

No. That is where my hon. friend is in error, I think. He and the hon. member for Lisgar as well as the hon. member for Weyburn, in all their arguments, assume that at once there will be an increase in the price of cream separators.
We do not assume that the increase will be at once-put it that way.
Well, the assumption is that as a result of this there will be an increase in price.
Put it that way.

But that does not follow at all. I showed last night that we were importing, for instance, from the United States and from Sweden large numbers of cream separators. Now, if we can increase production in Canada and absorb part of that, if we can give to Great Britain part of that business, does it not follow that there is likely to be a reduction? As a matter of fact I am told that in all probability there will be a reduction in the cost of production and therefore in the price of cream separators, as a result of increased production on the one hand and on the other-

In my estimation parliament ought to take pride in the industrial development of this country. We should take pride in that development, because as the Prime Minister intimated yesterday, every industry which is made successful means further assistance to the primary producer, the farmer, the lumberman and the miner. In a sense that is rather a strange question. It is just as I have indicated; these matters of prices are carefully kept track of, and the information is laid before the ministers and before the government. I think, of course, my hon. friend wants to know if there is any officer who is specifically instructed to keep a check on these prices and take action under any statute or regulation. I should say there is no officer with such a specific duty.

Before this item carries I think the house and the country might as well realize that it will mean an increase in the price of cream separators. In 1930 we had assurance from this government in connection with various commodities on which duties were increased; they told us that there would be no increase in prices. The government gave us to understand that they had the assurance in writing from the manufacturers that there would be no increase in price. We were led to believe that the government would assume the responsibility of removing the duties where prices were not reduced in accordance with world prices. We had that assurance from the Prime Minister and I would ask the government now whether anything has been done since 1930. I ask this house, has anything been done by this government since that time? They realized that they should take into consideration the fact that when world prices dropped there should be a corresponding drop in our own commodities. It has been drawn to the attention of the house by members at various times that there have been either increases or no reductions, and we are entitled to know what action has
been taken. In speaking of items that were dealt with in 1930, I will refer once again to oil products. The case was clearly proved. We had the definite assurance of the Prime Minister in 1930, but nothing was done and it does not appear to be the intention of this government to carry out the undertakings they gave the people. As regards the minister's assurance that there will be no increase in price, that is just so much more humbug, such as we got in 1930. Everyone who has listened to the discussion that has taken place on this and on other items under this agreement will realize that where there is an increase in duty there will be a consequent increase in price to the consumer, and the farmers who have to buy cream separators might just as well make up their minds right now that they will pay more for that commodity.

The British system is different from ours. I am glad my hon. friend raised that question because it reminds me of something I overlooked a few moments ago when he inquired what the British duty was on cream separators, and some of the other hon. gentlemen inquired with regard to parts. It must be borne in mind that Great Britain imposes its duties on a c.i.f. basis, which is a very much higher basis than we are on, ours being the f.o.b. basis. Take cream separators for instance. The Canadian duty would be imposed on the cost of the article in Great Britain. My hon. friend asks whether Great Britain has a dumping duty provision similar to ours. They have not the same provisions as we have. Great Britain operates its import act very largely by regulations under the treasury board, and broad general powers are given to that body. It is under the treasury board, the official being known as the Commissioner of Customs and Excise, and they invest the board and the commissioner with very wide powers. They have not the same dumping provisions as we have but, as we do, they insist upon a sworn declaration of the accuracy of the invoice, which must be in just as clear terms as we call for. And, of course, they have a provision for the imposition of

That puts us in this position then. Britain has no anti-dumping laws but she insists of course on a true and accurate invoice. But if the Swedish manufacturer of cream separators wishes to absorb the British duty and sell in Britain at the same price as he would sell in Sweden, he may do so. These separators cannot of course be transhipped to Canada, but the effect of that possibility to the Swedish manufacturer would be to force the British manufacturer in Great Britain to compete with the imported article, would it not? We should therefore find the price of separators in Britain coming down to the world level, and so the Canadian manufacturer who is looking for additional protection would find himself in competition with British separators selling at world prices. That would not hurt the farmer very much; he would not object to that. I want to look at the figures the minister gave last night. The other night tinplate-item 383, I believe-was under discussion. I should like to refer to an argument made yesterday by the Prime Minister and repeated in part this morning by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. $1,300,000,000 was consumed in Canada. I asked the Prime Minister if he had made any allowance for duplications, but he replied that he considered the figures to be correct. I took the trouble to check over these figures and I find that in order to find a year in which there was $1,600,000,000 worth of farm products produced in Canada, the Prime Minister had to go back to the days of the Liberal regime in 1929. The Prime Minister has evidently forgotten that there has been a change of government and that there is no such wealth produced today. Today the total value of farm products produced is $880,000,000, just about one-half what it was in 1929.
As far as consumption by the Canadian people is concerned, let us see what happens to this production before it reaches the people. Some 3,000,000 horses have to be fed, some 8.000,000 cattle have to be fed, some
3,600,000	sheep have to be fed, some 4,700,000 swine and 65,000,000 poultry have to be fed; all these animals have to be fed before the people of Canada get a chance at this production. The Prime Minister simply took the gross value of all farm products produced in Canada and said that that is what we consume; he forgot that the hay is destroyed in producing milk, that the milk is destroyed in producing butter and cream and that the only thing that counts is the final product. I suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that when they refer to a possible market for our farm products they take pains to see where the stuff is consumed.

I think the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Yallance) made a very reasonable request when he asked that the government, through the Minister of National Revenue, allow cream separators to come in under the present duty without any interference by the placing thereon of an arbitrary value. The Minister of National Revenue is in his seat and I should like to get some assurance from him that this reasonable request will be acceded to. Before I

take my seat may I say to my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) that the only reason I mentioned the eastern townships was that I spent a very pleasant week-end there last year, and the people were so kind to me that I could not forget them.

When speaking on the agreement as a whole I indicated that I thought this particular item was from our point of view the worst item in the whole schedule. I singled it out as the one which in my opinion would be the most difficult for the government to defend. It has been stated by the ministers who are representing the government and defending this agreement that all arguments from this side of the house are based wholly on the assumption that prices will be increased. It has been indicated, and I think quite correctly, that the final proof will be supplied by the actual circumstances that arise. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. That of course is true. It is equally true as applied to any other item or any other piece of legislation brought down in this house dealing with conditions with which we have not had previous experience. But in making an assumption it is reasonable to ask, is it based upon logic, upon experience in other lines which might well be applied to the particular case before us? That is about all we can do. As a matter of fact, the government itself is assuming just as much as anybody else when they say that there will not be a price increase. The question is, what are the logical grounds for the assumption? All discussion would be wholly useless were we to accept the situation that we must wait and see. We cannot do that.
What are the facts? They are well known, and have been reiterated so often that I do not care to repeat them. Cream separators have come in free for many years. Now a certain condition has arisen and a duty of 25 per cent is being placed on all separators coming in from any country outside the British Empire. We turn to past years and find that a number of years ago Britain exported quite a substantial number of separators to this country. That business was stopped during the war because the factory was turned over to other purposes, and during the last few years no separators have entered this country from Britain. What are we to assume by that? We can only assume that at the price which is being paid for separators in Canada the British did not find it profitable to compete. In view of the fact that for the last five years Great Britain has been combing the earth looking for opportunities to increase her export trade in every direction, we can only conclude that she has not sold separators

United Kingdom.
in this country because she could not sell them at the price fixed by competition in this country. I think we can accept that.
The purpose of this new provision is twofold, and both purposes are perfectly legitimate. One is to permit Great Britain to sell a number of separators here, increasing her business by means of the preference. The other purpose is to enable the manufacturers of Canada to sell a larger proportion of their separators. The result anticipated by the minister is that there will be a greater output of separators on the part of both Great Britain and Canada, and that with that greater output the chances are in favour of a possible reduction in the price. Is that likely to be the case? Time alone will show. But to my mind, going upon the facts we have, as Great Britain has not been able to sell separators in Canada at present prices, it seems to me that only one of two things can happen: Either the Canadian manufacturer takes the whole market and in view of his larger output is able to continue to sell at present prices, or else prices will rise to a sufficient extent to allow Great Britain to sell separators at a profit in this country. Those are the only two alternatives.
As to the former, that Canadian manufacturers may supply the entire market at present prices, so long as they supply the separators we want and they are of good quality, I do not think exception can be taken to that. But why bring that in as part of this agreement? That would be no good to Great Britain. The only possible benefit that can come from this to Great Britain is from an increased price. I think we are warranted in assuming that, and therefore I think the argument which has been advanced as to the weight which this imposes on the dairy industry is well founded. True, it is only an assumption but I think it is a reasonable one.
The statement has been made that as a counterbalancing factor the price of repair parts will be lower than it was. If that be true, it will apply, of course, to those separators which are sold in the future. Just what value would a lower price on repair parts be tc the farmer w'ho owns a separator if those repair parts can only come from Great Britain and are not suitable for the farmer's purpose and the machine he now has? If you practically exclude repair parts from the country which made the separator, the lower price of the repair parts does not help the farmer at all.

My hon. friend will bear
in mind that while repair parts enter free from Great Britain, the duty on repair parts from 5371J-83
all other countries has been decreased very substantially.

Precisely, and to that
extent undoubtedly it may be of some benefit to the farmer. In conclusion, without taking up any more time, I can only make the assertion that I look upon this item as not only unwise but unfair, as one which it will be most difficult to explain and defend in the country, and looking to the future I think we can only anticipate a higher price. It is one item to which I, in common with others, take great exception, believing it to be unnecessary as well as unwise. I might be asked, why then did I vote for the agreement? I voted for it, as I stated before, because against its disadvantages there must be offset the advantages of the British market for our butter and dairy products. You have to balance one against the other. But I do not think it is necessary to give with the one hand and take awiay with the other. If the farmer of this country requires a wider market for his products I think it is unfair to give him that with the one hand, and then partially deprive him of the benefit by taking away something with the other hand.

In response to a question which I asked a few minutes ago the minister stated that this was a matter of government policy and therefore the National Dairy Council had not been consulted. I presume that would also apply so far as the British government is concerned. But I notice that in the schedule, under article one, free entry is provided into the British market for our butter and cheese and other milk products for three years certain. After that it is uncertain. That to me is a clear indication that the British government must have consulted their agricultural interests. In another article of the agreement reference is made to bacon and ham and pork products, and the provisions of that article are subject to a report to be made by a commission which is investigating farming conditions in Great Britain. I am convinced that the farmers of Canada have had a raw deal. They have knocked at the doors of the government asking to make representations so that the great industry of agriculture might receive some benefits and, at least on one occasion, they were refused. I point out that this government might better have left these two items of barbed wire and cream separators off the list entirely, because no maitter what their explanations may be the farmers are feeling they are being imposed upon by what the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton) has described as a great

At the same time their farm produce, the only commodity they have to sell, is selling at ridiculously low prices. I have been called to my feet by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien). In answer I state that we are dealing with an agreement the terms of which must be kept. But if there is unfair trade and the government is in a position to act, it will most certainly use any instrument which comes to hand to prevent such a condition. For many years of my life I have been connected with the cream separator business. I am only sorry the Hon. Thomas Low, late Minister of Trade and Commerce in this house, was not present because he would bear out the further remarks I have to make.
I have been debating in my own mind whether some of the information I am about to disclose is of such a confidential character that I should not give it to the committee. I have decided however to state the facts as I know them. If any person tells you that this tariff change was sought by manufacturers, do not believe it. The statement has been made that they did not seek it, and I wish to add my testimony to that effect. Let me say also that the business in cream separators is diversified throughout the whole world, and yet it is in very few hands. A situation arose when it was more important for manufacturers of cream separators in Canada not to manufacture, but to import from the United States. There are two such concerns with establishments both here and in the United States. Another cream separator company stated it was unfair that cream separators and parts should be free for the manufacturer, and yet a duty levied upon the farmers. Therefore there was the situation of one company being willing to take the protection, and the other company unwilling. As the Hon. Thomas Low could tell you that condition continued. If a duty on cream separators had been asked from previous administrations I am sure, owing to the strength of opinion which would have supported it, that duty would have been granted. Now, what will be the effect of this tariff change?

The effect of the agreement with the United Kingdom representatives is that cream separators and parte thereof enter free. I feel satisfied if hon. members would examine the invoices in our custom houses they would find that the most important importer of cream separators and parts has been a company doing business in Canada. That will not continue, because that company-and a strong company it is-is quite able to manufacture those parts in Canada. This country, instead of the United States, will reap the benefit of such business. As the industry well knows, that is a plain fact.
Then, as to price: Do not believe that there is any danger of higher prices, because competition is now keen. These manufacturing concerns in Canada can manufacture at as low a price as they can manufacture in the United States. The suggestion may be offered that a greater market would give them an advantage in the United States, but I am suggesting that the two big concerns can tune up and give the farmer of Canada a cream separator at the price he is now paying. There will be no occasion for raising prices, and I feel sure the competition is so keen they will not be raised.
The minister has mentioned two large companies. Will they not tune together, and thereby exact greater prices from the farmers?

There is just as little
likelihood of their tuning together as there is of my agreement with my hon. friend opposite. I know that in the British Empire there is a factory which is subsidiary to the major factory situated in Sweden. But when we speak of factories in Sweden, the United States and Finland we must remember they are_ all under one control; we are speaking merely of a main company with subsidiaries. I assure the committee that in my opinion this, on balance, is all to the good. There is that anomaly with regard to parts which, I submit, is unfair, and I do not think any hon. member of the house could reasonably defend it. That is wiped out. Parts will come to the farmer at lower prices brought about by competition. The business which formerly, for convenience sake, was done in the United States, will be done in Canada.
Why was one of these manufacturing concerns strongly opposed to a duty on cream separators? Because, powerful as they were, they were manufacturing other dairy machines which were going into the United States duty free. They said, "Do not disturb the present situation, because if you do there will be trouble." This representation was not

reunited. Kingdom
made to the Conservative party, but to hon. members opposite when in power. But, on balance, in my view this is all to the good.

If the minister disturbs the relationship in existence between the company he has mentioned and their export business to the United States, would he not expect they would lose a certain amount of Canadian business as a result.

I think we will lose no
Canadian business at all; in fact I think we will gain more.

We have heard so much discussion on this cream separator item that I am led to wonder how we may expect Englishmen to export cream separators to Canada. Looking at the records we find that we have been exporting to Great Britain a large number of cream separators, and Great Britain has been exporting none to Canada, notwithstanding the fact that British cream separators were entitled to come in here free, as they will continue to be so entitled. What is going to arise to enable Great Britain to ship cream separators here? They will be on the same basis as they were before, they have been free, they are going to be free. The fact is that the article made in Great Britain has not been favoured by Canadians, that is the whole story.

About a dollar a year; so he may make a saving of five cents a year. But he will have to pay more for the separator. few remarks to make on this item. Perhaps I could do it much better after we resume.

No, Mr. Chairman. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion on this item, and particularly to the statement made by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this tariff increase will not increase the price of the finished article. That is an argument that has been used by the government in defence of other increases in the tariff, and in order to bolster up that argument they frequently point to the fact that there have been no increases in the prices of manufactured products in Canada since they came into office. Perhaps that argument is good, but let me point out to the government that there has been a tremendous falling off in prices all along the line since this government came to power, and that the spread between the primary and secondary products is much wider than ever before. Undoubtedly that is the result of the protection received by the manufacturing industry of Canada.
In connection with the cream separator industry may I say that I cannot conceive any reason why this industry needs any particular protection. I do not know any good reason that can be suggested as to why it should receive protection. We do know that the British manufacturer, as has been very properly pointed out by several hon. gentlemen on this side of the house, is manufacturing the larger sizes of separators used in large creameries, and that even their own requirements are supplied from foreign sources. I think it is evident that they will have to reorganize their industry at least if they are to actively compete with Canadian manufacturers. Not only do this government persist in giving protection to Canadian manufacturers almost to the point of exclusion; they take the opposite course when the raw products used by the same manufacturers are in question, and that is what has happened here. The raw products which enter into the manufacture of cream separators have been reduced pretty well all along the line, and the argument that repair parts for the separators now in use by the farmers of Canada will be cheaper does not mean very much. That saving will amount to very little in the case of the average farmer who purchases these repair parts. One thing is sure, as the hon. member for Lisgar said; when the government increased the protection on farm implement parts, repair parts manufactured by indepen-

dent industries who did not manufacture the complete article went up in price. There may be some reduction in these parts, but it will be very slight. The fact remains, and it has been self-evident throughout the discussion on tariff matters, that these increases will raise the price paid by the consumer. It seems to me nothing more need be said in that connection.
Hon. gentlemen opposite argued formerly t-hat by increasing the tariff we created more employment for people in Canada, and in consequence created a larger consuming public for our natural products. If there were any possibility of creating a secondary industry in this country that could consume all the farm and manufactured products there might be something in that argument, but by no process of reasoning can it be argued that we are even within measurable distance of that state of affairs. Moreover, it does not help even in countries where they can almost consume all their own products; on the contrary it has created a very difficult situation for the consumers in those countries, and in general has helped create more unemployment. So the argument put forward by hon. gentlemen opposite that this change will be beneficial to anyone-that is, anyone but the manufacturers of cream separators in Canada-has no basis. Undoubtedly those manufacturers will take advantage of the protection they are afforded. I have watched this process of the application of tariffs fairly closely, because it is one of the things in which I have been very greatly interested. As I said the other day, I know of only one industry in Canada that has not taken and is not taking full advantage of the protection afforded them. I refer to the rubber industry. Hon. gentlemen may argue that to the extent of three or four per cent other industries do not take that advantage, but why are protective duties necessary?
Hon. gentlemen opposite have stated in connection with this particular item-I believe it was the Prime Minister who made the statement-that the Canadian manufacturer of cream separators could compete with the American manufacturer, that he could produce an article equal in value at an equal cost. I think he stated that the Canadian manufacturers had so perfected their organizations in Canada that the same separator was selling wholesale for at least $28 less in Canada than in the United States. In the next breath he said he would have to admit that the importation from the United States into Canada was very considerable. No, Mr. Chairman,

every time you increase the tariff on a given product you can be dead sure that the consumers who purchase the goods will have to pay almost the whole of that increase.
If there is an increase.

I wonder if the
minister realizes that this increase of ten per cent in intermediate and general affects, practically speaking, one province only, the province of Quebec. As the minister very well knows, the teaching in our medical schools in Quebec is based entirely on the French method and the teaching in the French universities. as far as our universities and medical schools are concerned, have been taught in French universities; the descriptions of surgical operations contained in our technical books, including the instruments used, are altogether French. The students, the doctors graduating from these universities have been taught the French instrumentation. They have been taught nothing else. First they are taught the methods and then the use of the instruments, and you are simply exacting a premium from the practice of medicine and surgery in the province of Quebec. I mention Quebec particularly because we are practically the only province where French methods and French teaching are entirely followed. These surgical instruments include needles, x-ray instruments and microscopes. Do you realize that in our French universities and medical schools, as well as our French Canadian hospitals, and even in those medical units that have been organized recently, French instruments are used exclusively? We cannot exchange them for one very good reason. Two-thirds of the medical practitioners in the province of Quebec, especially those practising in the rural communities, do not read or understand English. Therefore it is impossible for them to substitute surgical instruments manufactured either in England or in the United States for the French instruments they have been using in the past, and it seems to me this legislation is going to place a great handicap on a profession which already is extremely handicapped in these times of stress. For these people a 10 per cent increase will make the price almost prohibitive as far as the purchase of French instruments is concerned. Surely the government is not so poor that by means of the tariff they must tax our universities, our hospitals, our medical men and so on. I am under the impression that under the heading of surgical instruments will come even those instruments which are used in our colleges for teaching the pupils. They are all of French manufacture, and the reason these articles were free under all tariffs in the past -was because of the fact that Quebec is in an extremely awkward situation in this respect. So I say that this tariff is simply a premium levied against our French Canadian medical profession.

the time of the committee discussing this matter but I was asked by a medical friend, rather a well known man, whether I would present this statement to the committee as a matter of general principle applicable to questions such as the one now under consideration. His view is that in connection with instruments or medicine or any of those things upon which the lives and the health of the people directly depend, the first consideration should be not any question of business, not any question affecting the individual or the country producing or selling the commodity required, but that rather, in matters where the lives and the health of the people are directly concerned, the sole consideration should be the ability of those who require such instruments to get them where they can best be procured and at the cheapest price. We have never had explained in this house the reason why arrangements of this kind should be made. Why, I ask, should we give preferential treatment to the textile industries? There are many other lines of business that are practically bankrupt, some of them absolutely so. We have been trying to point out from this corner of the house that the great wheat industry is in a very bad way in the west; in fact the agricultural industry all over Canada is in a bad way, with many farms mortgaged and some of them threatened with foreclosure. I am sure that does not work out at all in relation to wage costs. My hon. friend will recall that this afternoon I pointed out that the abnormal conditions with which industry generally was confronted when we came into office made necessary emergency treatment, and the treatment we gave this section of the tariff was the result of this emergent condition. I also pointed out to my hon. friend that we did not look upon this as a permanent condition of the tariff; we felt that it was necessary to take extraordinary methods to prevent the closing down of these important industries, and we achieved that end. As I pointed out this afternoon, we were confronted with two alternatives; one was to let the industry in Canada go, and the other was to take some steps that would adequately protect it against the dumping of goods from abroad, bankrupt stocks, distress sales and so on. What is the price of overalls today?

It would take what we call a butcher hog to buy a pair of overalls in Alberta, and it takes six months to produce that hog, which requires a good deal of feed during that period. There is one other question I want to ask. Considering the amount of tariff protection that is to be allowed the Canadian textile manufacturers, based on the difference in the cost of production in the two countries, is it the intention of the government that allowance should be made in the returns of capital stock of the textile companies now operating in Canada, or will action be taken to squeeze out some of the water in these stocks, similar to the action which the minister told us was taken in England in regard to one of the large cotton concerns there. The way my hon. friend puts the question makes it impossible to give an answer directly. That would be very difficult, because September is precisely in the middle of the fiscal year and all statistics are compiled for the fiscal year. The only way we could get that information would be to put a staff on to segregate these items month by month and invoice by invoice. It could not be obtained except with considerable difficulty.

I understand the minister's difficulty, but I should like to have this information in order to discover the effect upon our importations of the exchange adjustment duty, as the minister likes to call it, which was imposed after Great Britain went off the gold standard. It i3 very difficult to arrive at the exact rates, but as nearly as we can figure them, the total duty will average something over fifty per cent. The total production of Canada is valued at $58,000,000, and fifty per cent of this amount would represent the increase in price made by the domestic manufacturers. This will give some idea of what this industry is costing Canada. We are told that it pays $14,500,000 in wages. That is so much to the good; that is something to be put to the credit of the industry, but, on the other hand, we want to know what this industry is costing us. If they are charging fifty per cent more than the goods are worth, then I would say that this industry which pays $14,500,000 in wages is costing us between $25,000,000 and $30,000,000 in increased prices.
It is about time that we began to take stock of our industries in order to find out which ones are profitable and which ones are not. Any industry which is not selfsupporting and which cannot compete with the world, any industry which has to come to the government and ask permission to charge an extra price for its goods, is not worth while, even in these hard times. It is a parasite living upon the rest of the community. It is said that we must take care of these industries, that we must take care of the widows and orphans who have invested their money therein, but I am more concerned with the widows and orphans who have no money to invest in any industry, who have no clothing to wear and who cannot buy even the cheapest cotton goods. Last June the Minister of National Revenue told us how he would not let an importer bring in ten thousand dozen cheap ladies' dresses to be sold in Canada at three for a dollar, but today there are many of our people who cannot afford to pay even this low price.
I should like to deal for a moment with the quality of goods now being put upon the market. When you shut out foreign and 53719-85
British competition, and it has been shut out, and deliver the market into the hands of a Canadian monopoly, that monopoly is more than likely to deteriorate the quality of their goods as well as to increase the price. Canadian women have been accustomed to buying cheap house dresses which they wear for a day or two and then wash. I am told that the dress on the market today is so poorly dyed that the colours run as soon as they are put into water. When I see how this tariff is built up of all these varying factors I am reminded of a story of a number of college students who wished to play a joke on their professor. They took the body of one insect, the legs of another, the head of a third, and the wings of a fourth, glued them all together and submitted the result to the professor for identification. He looked at the insect, adjusted his glasses, frowned, and then, "Ah", he said, "I see it is a humbug". I think, Mr. Chairman, this tariff, made up as it is of ad valorem duties, specific duties, exchange dumping duties, the excise tax, the sales tax and as many other things as the commissioner of customs and his assistants can think of, might well be described as a humbug.
The minister said a moment ago that they had actually reduced the duty on the item we are discussing. Reduced the duty from what? From what it was when they were through with it last year. Take item 523b. Here are the rates as they have been and as they are to-day. In 1895 the preferential rate on this item was 234 per cent; in 1907, 25 per cent; 1923, 18 per cent; September, 1930, after the short session, 224 per cent, and an additional three cents a yard, which made it approximately 27 per cent. In the fall of 1931, after Great Britain had gone off the gold standard, the rate suddenly jumped to 61 per cent. And now, after the imperial conference, in order to encourage interimperial trade, we have lowered the duty from 61 to 58.5 per cent, and the minister tells us that he has lowered the duties from where

we left them! We left them at 18 per cent. The government opposite have twice since then increased them, last year to 61 per cent Now they have reduced that rate to 58 per cent, and the minister says it is done to encourage British trade!

Once more I ask: What is this industry giving in exchange for that? Sixty per cent added to the $58,000,000 worth of goods produced in Canada, and $14,000,000 paid in wages? Mr. Chairman, this industry is a luxury we cannot afford; we cannot afford to continue it.

He is permitting them to charge us an extra sixty per cent for our cotton goods and permitting the woollen interests to charge an extra price for their goods. He is permitting every other manufacturing industry to add to the price we have to pay for goods they have to sell. The minister's statement is surprising. Canadian wool was never as cheap as it is at the present time. The clip in western Canada is practically all in the hands of the producers because they cannot sell it at any price nor can they give it away. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are all agreed on that.

I was very much struck, in reference to this matter, by certain figures I saw in the Monthly Bulletin of Agricultural Statistics for March, 1932. There a comparison is given of prices paid for wool. The prices were, for the years from 1922 on, as follows:

Then it falls to 11 and 8 and now it is about 4 or 5 cents per pound. I am always struck by something which appears to me to be incongruous in the tariff I am not here to advocate a high tariff on wool or on anything else, but I must remind hon. gentlemen opposite that this government promised the

United Kingdom
farmers to make tariffs fight for them; yet this is the most iniquitous tariff one could imagine. In the United States the tariff on wool is very high. I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I believe that the specific tariff was adopted in the United States for the purpose of carrying out the tariff which was given to the farmers on wool. In Canada our specific tariff is nearly as high as the specific tariff which was put into force in the United States to take care of the tariff imposed there on wool, but we have no tariff at all on wool. This is the most iniquitous provision that has ever been made in our tariff. No consideration whatever is given the farmer. One would expect that the woollen manufacturers of Canada would at least use Canadian wool. We produce about one quarter of the wool that is used in Canada. Now, when our tariff was increased to the extreme limit, skyhigh, with the specific duty and everything else afforded the manufacturer, no consideration whatever was given the farmer except talk. On July 14, 1931, I drew the attention of the Prime Minister to this very fact. Later on, during the course of last session, the Minister of Finance himself stood up and said that some consideration should be shown the wool growers. I have read many letters in this house from cooperative organizations like the Wool Growers' Association, which is a very influential body in this dominion, and the sheepbreeders in convention in Toronto have passed resolutions and forwarded letters to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, all with reference to this subject. The Prime Minister, in answer to my poor utterances, said, "Give us time." He gave us some hope, but we have been given hope so many times that now we should like to see something practical done. If the manufacturers had a little heart they would take at least one-quarter of their wool supplies from the wool producers in Canada. We produce about 20,000,000 pounds of wool, using round figures, and the consumption in Canada is about 80,000,000 pounds. In the Monthly Bulletin of Agricultural Statistics for March, 1932, I read the following:
Wool prices were again below the previous year by at least 25 per cent. Although the woolen manufacturers are expanding their business in Canada, there has apparently been little, if any, increase in the use of Canadian wools by Canadian manufacturers. During the year 4,769,574 pounds were exported to Britain. The wools which are being exported are among Canada's best and very favourable comments are being received in regard to the quality of the product as represented in Canada's officially graded wools.
And quoting again from the same bulletin:
The wool clip in 1931 was of good quality. The expansion of the use of purebred rams was reflected in a further refinement within the official grades. There was very little local buying of wool and prices for ungraded wools ranged from five to eight cents per pound.
And again:
Canadian mills continue to use a limited volume of home-grown wool.
I do not want to press this matter too strongly at the moment, but when the question comes up again I hope to take part in the discussion. This government has pledged itself to do something for the farmer. Take fertilizer, for instance. We soon realize the advantages which are given to the manufacturer. The same thing applies to wool; the farmer receives no consideration from the government or from the manufacturer. He receives only four to five cents per pound for his product, while the manufacturer benefits by a specific and ad valorem duty. If I am not in error, I understand that in the United States a specific duty alone is considered all that is necessary in the way of a tariff on wool. It is considered that about two and a half to three pounds of virgin wool is required to make one pound of manufactured cloth, so that the tariff on wool is about one-third of the specific tariff on cloth. I wish the minister would give us some hope of possible relief to our farmers.

Quite so. I think it should be recognized that Canadian blanket manufacturing is really one of the most efficient industries in the country. A marvellously fine article is turned out, I think at a reasonable price.

eminent. They are using very little Canadian wool. No more glaring example could be found of the extraordinary lengths to which the government have gone in soaking the Canadian consumer of wearing apparel, something that we need and must have in Canada, and which the government know we must have. And then they tell us that this is done in order to preserve the industry! Why, Mr. Chairman, if you counted every man who is engaged in this industry in Canada today you would not get a total more than 40,000, and I venture to say that in a generous estimate. We have
700,000	people out of work, and the government is asking them to pay this exorbitant price for wearing apparel which they must have in a climate like ours. It is tariff-making gone mad. The excuse which the government give that woollen mills in this country have been revived by the tariff does not hold water. We cannot get a reasonable price for our wool; for these mills are not using Canadian wood. Wool is in just the same predicament as butter and eggs, which this government undertook to increase in price to the producer. In every instance the Canadian consumer is the loser. In connection with secondary industries we find that tariffs are clamped on which force him to pay exorbitant prices for the goods he must use. With the single exception of the small woollen manufacturer I would say that the textile industry was getting along pretty well on the protection they enjoyed during the ten years the previous government held office. They were making splendid progress and did not need this extra assistance. No one can convince me there is any necessity for the exorbitant tariffs on textiles provided by this government.
I hope the government will appoint a tariff board; I hope the textile industries will be investigated before that board, and that it will have some conception of what is reasonable, just and fair as between producer and consumer. Of all the increases hon. members opposite have made this is the worst. [DOT] The government has not given the British manufacturer the slightest chance to get into the Canadian market; he is being offered no greater advantage than he possessed under the tariffs of 1930 and 1931. The small re-

ductions on cotton textiles, as they appear in the schedule, mean very little, and will be of no benefit to the British manufacturer. I say here and now that Great Britain has been one of the best customers for Canadian natural products. Here is one set of items in the schedule from which Great Britain could have received some benefit; we would have been giving something back, but hon. gentlemen have chosen to ignore any such arrangement. The marvel to me is that the British delegation treated us so generously at the recent conference. I cannot understand it. In connection with articles which they can manufacture, and with which they can enter into competition on the world market, they are not given a chance to compete in the Canadian market. In commodities the trade in which amounts to little or nothing, and on certain raw products, some chance is given to Great Britain, but very little. I am interested in the consumers of Canada, those men and women who will have to pay and pay dearly as they have done on every occasion that a policy of extreme protection has been put into effect. Particularly is that true in connection with articles of clothing.

From the United Kingdom the imports in 1931 were valued at 8538,000 and in 1932 at $196,000. The idea behind this tariff is the entire prohibition of imports. The hon. member who has just taken his seat has stated that the present prices in Canada are low. I direct his attention to the fact that that condition is not peculiar to Canada but obtains throughout the world, and applies to all commodities. Under the guise of a British preference, and with an imperial agreement
before us, we are locking the door more securely than ever against Great Britain in connection with textiles. We are locking the door against imports from Great Britain; the Minister of Finance and Minister of Trade and Commerce know it. Nothing in this agreement has caused so much vexation and irritation in the old country as the fact that we have refused to give them a decent chance to sell their textiles. I agree with my hon. friend when he states that we should do anything we can to provide labour and promote industry in Canada. But the price is too high. For the last two years, for reasons not difficult to analyze, this government has shown special favouritism to the textile industry of Canada. If hon. members wish I shall analyze that favouritism.
Go ahead.

The
Dominion Textile Company have received more favours from this government in the last two years than any other single industry in Canada.
Has it cost you anything?

Yes, and every consumer in the Dominion of Canada. I will tell my hon. friend that the tariff schedule as applied to the textile industry in Canada is not justified by any law of economics, fair play or common sense, and the consumer of Canada is paying for it. If you look at your importations of textiles from the old country during the last three or four years you will see that the door has been gradually closed on textiles from the old country, building up a monopoly in Canada. When you create a monopoly for an industry in Canada you are imposing a burden on the consumer. I want to tell my hon. friends that the big problem today in Canada, far bigger than any item in this agreement, is that of trying to look after the hundreds of thousands-800,000 we were told by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) the other day -who are under or in need of relief; yet the poor man who wants to buy an overcoat or any textile fabric is penalized by these tariffs. Why is this in the imperial conference agreement? Is it to promote imperial trade? Will any hon. member on the other side will dare to say that this is promoting British trade? Look at the figures for the last three or four years, and you will see, whether you will approve, as do hon. members on that side of the house, or disapprove, as we do, that year by year you are closing the door against the importation of British textile fabrics into Canada. Under the guise of promoting British

It is the same description as appears in the tariff so far as the words "crude petroleum not in its natural state" are concerned. Some describe it as skinned. It has been put through some slight process.
Does the minister think that one cent per gallon is enough protection to meet the competition from Soviet Russia?
This is what they asked for.

I notice that at the top of the column it says "margin of preference over intermediate tariff" and under item 267b in the present tariff this crude petroleum comes in under four-tenths of a cent intermediate. A margin of preference of one cent per gallon would mean a reduction below that, would it not?

This is simply meant to give a preference of one cent a gallon. If my hon. friend will look at the statutory provision in the votes and proceedings he will find there that the rate is a half a cent, and then a cent and a half.

Under 267B?

Yes. It carries out the understanding set forth in schedule F.
Is this particular item aimed at Russian and Roumanian oil which has been imported into this country?
It is not aimed at anything except to give Trinidad access to our market, and this is the manner in which they have asked that it should be done.
