This is an item which was requested by the British particularly on behalf of the colonies. Formerly the rates were free across the board. Cocoanut oil is produced very largely in the different colonies, and it is a product in which they feel they can do a very large business.

Unless it be for revenue purposes, I cannot see why a duty was placed on it at all.

catch the significance of it when it was discussed in schedule E, but if it is going to come from empire countries-and I believe there is no hope of producing it in Canada-I cannot see why there should be a duty at all. This commodity is growing in use. Unless the minister desires revenue I can see no reason why it should not be free.

On article 9:
His Majesty's government in Canada will invite parliament to pass the legislation necessary to substitute for the duties of customs now leviable on the goods specified in schedule E the duties shown in that schedule, provided that nothing in this article shall preclude His Majesty's government in Canada from reducing the duties specified in the said schedule so long as the margin of British preference shown in that schedule is preserved or from increasing the rates under the intermediate or general tariff set out in the said schedule.
I understood the Minister of Finance to say he had two or three amendments to move.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not necessary to move them until we reach committee of ways and means.
Article 9 agreed to.
On article 10:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that protection by tariffs shall be afforded against United Kingdom products only to those industries which are reasonably assured of sound opportunities for success.

I should like either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Trade and Commerce to explain to the committee the significance of the following phrase:
Only to those industries which are reasonably assured of sound opportunities for success.
What will be the guiding maxim for determining the opportunities for success or prospects of success in each case?

This afternoon a discussion which took place on one of the items was very much along the same line. I read to the committee part of the Tariff Board Act indicating the principle upon which the tariff board would proceed. This is simply an assurance to the British government that in arriving at the tariffs to be imposed in this country protection shall not be put into effect beyond the point indicated herein, namely, that point where the industry has a reasonable opportunity of success. The language in the article is as clear as it could be made.
Article 10 agreed to.
On article 11:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that during the currency of this agreement the tariff shall be based on the principle that protective duties shall not exceed such a level as will give United Kingdom producers full opportunity of reasonable competition on the basis of the relative cost of economical and efficient production, provided that in the application of such principle special consideration shall be given to the ease of industries not fully established.

In connection. with article 11 I should like to have a declaration of policy from one of the ministers in regard to the significance of the following proviso:
. . . provided that in the application of such principle special consideration shall be given to the case of industries not fully established.
And in regard to the preceding expression:
. . . full opportunity of reasonable competition on the basis of the relative cost of economical and efficient production.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Ontario and other hon. members at an earlier stage in the debate, this is an antiquated provision which has been in the United States tariff for years. I should like to refer to an analysis of this provision which appears in the Ottawa supplement of The Economist for Saturday, October 22, 1932. Article 11 is quoted, and then the following comment appears:
This statement of principle, which is, of course, by no means new, looks at first sight to be very fair and just. But, on further examination, it will be found to be not only misleading but vicious; for while it appears to be a limiting principle, it is not a limitation either in theory or in practice; for if carried out strictly it would put an end to all foreign trade. Clearly, if a duty is put on equal to this difference, there will be no benefit from foreign trade, which is only advantageous because you can buy abroad cheaper than you can produce at home, and vice versa as regards exports. Practice confirms this theoretical conclusion. The doctrine was embodied by congress in the American Tariff Acts many years ago as an instruction to the American Tariff Commission. One of the earliest members of that commission, charged with the duty of carrying out this policy, wrote a book on "Making the Tariff in the United States" in which he pointed out the practical difficulty of carrying out this doctrine. Here are some of his conclusions: 

"The application of the difference between costs as a measure of duties is usually impossible owing to the difficulty of finding what the difference amounts to. Even if cost data were reliable the fact would remain that there is in every country more than one cost at which any commodity is produced in commercial quantities. The difficulties in obtaining and verifying costs of production are infinitely greater in foreign countries than they are in the United States. The conclusion cannot be escaped that it is rarely possible to ascertain accurately the difference in cost of production at home and abroad. To use as the basis of a general tariff act a thing so fleeting, evasive, and shadowy would be neither right nor possible."
The result was precisely what might have been expected, for, under the operation of this famous clause, practically every change has been upward; the only exceptions being of such small importance as to be derisory. The principle

United. Kingdom
has for many years past been used as a justification for the highest tariffs in the world. When the French delegates attempted to introduce it at the World conference of 1927 as a basis for rationalizing tariffs, it was rejected out of hand.
In practice no country has ever been able to carry out this so-called "scientific principle" in tariff making, but has used its discretion as to the extent to Which it will allow goods to come in subject to the penalty of a protective duty, and how far it will go towards excluding them altogether.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is out of order.

From
your point of view, Mr. Chairman, it may be out of order, but from our point of view these comments are relevant to the article under consideration.
It is instructive.

The
article in The Economist is instructive; it is logical, it is rational, it is moderate in tone. It points out that this antiquated provision embodied in the tariff structure of the United States is condemned by those who are most familiar with its terms and provisions. The article which I have read goes on to say that it is entirely impossible as a matter of determination of the principle of a scientific tariff to operate as provided in this clause. I should like to ask either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Trade and Commerce if they will be good enough in the first place to explain to the committee their conception of the significance of this provision, and in the second place to give their view as to the possibility of working it out in practice.

I think I can answer my hon. friend very clearly. I will give him an illustration that we have just dealt with in this schedule, namely, the linen industry. It was concluded that the linen industry, as regards all branches except the one we mentioned a short time ago, the production of crash towels and so on, was one which, while there were two or three factories struggling along, was not likely to become established in Canada. So we put linen on the free list and abandoned the attempt to establish that industry. There is an illustration of our interpretation of that very principle.

But my hon. friend is dealing with the other section. The section
to which my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre has referred contains another principle altogether.
I am quite aware of what he referred to.

My hon. friend did not answer the question. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre was pointing out that it was difficult to find out what the cost of production was in other countries, and he was asking how the government proposed to ascertain what the relative cost of economical and efficient production was in England as compared with Canada.

I think the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and I understand each other quite well. My hon. friend asked me how I would explain the phrase:
. . . provided that in the application of such principle special consideration shall be given to the case of industries not fully established.
That was the first point.

The answer is that we
found no difficulty in deciding that a given industry which had been trying to establish itself here for some time had not succeeded in doing so, and in the schedules passed tonight we dealt with it by placing it on the free list. That is an illustration of how the government views the application of that principle. My hon. friend referred to economical and efficient production. I have already intimated that in the Tariff Board Act we have set forth the principles there applicable; before my hon. friend came in I had read the relevant provision from the act. Certain, principles set forth for the guidance of the board covering labour conditions, cost of material, inquiry into the efficiency of management, and so on, and these will be the guiding principles by which we shall determine what is an economically and efficiently managed industry.

My hon. friend, I am afraid, has just reversed the real situation as it appears in this section. The proviso at the end of the section is that even though the cost of economical and efficient production is greater in Canada than in England, the government reserves to itself the right to continue the protection given to the industries concerned. My hon. friend gives the example of an industry not fully established, and
Questions

points out that in such a case the duty was taken off. We are more interested in the industries to which special consideration is being given because of the fact that they are not fully established. How does my hon. friend propose to find out whether an industry qualifies under this proviso?
I have already intimated that the test will be applied by the tariff board under the principles clearly set forth in the Tariff Board Act.

Item agreed to.
